baseRef.description: Ref the range starts at. The commits checked are `<baseRef>..HEAD`.

conventional-commits.name: Commits follow Conventional Commits
conventional-commits.description: Every commit message in the build range follows the Conventional Commits specification, including the subject line, the blank line before the body, and the BREAKING CHANGE footer.
conventional-commits.remediation: Rewrite each offending commit message as `type(scope): description`, for example `fix(api): reject expired tokens`. The scope is optional, but if you give one it must name something. A `!` before the colon marks a breaking change, and the colon is followed by a space and a description. The body starts after one blank line, and a breaking change described in the footer is written as `BREAKING CHANGE: <description>`, in uppercase. See the [Conventional Commits specification](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/).

types.description: Types accepted before the colon, as a regular expression alternation.

no-merge-commits.name: No merge commits
no-merge-commits.description: The build range contains no merge commits.
no-merge-commits.remediation:
Rebase your branch onto the base ref instead of merging into it:

```bash
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
```

See [Git Branching: Rebasing](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Branching-Rebasing).

work-item-reference.name: Commits reference a work item
work-item-reference.description: Every commit in the build range, or the branch it is on, references the change record it belongs to.
work-item-reference.remediation:
Put the ticket key in the commit subject or body, or in the branch name:

```
feat(ledger): round half to even on settlement

Refs: COMPANY-1423
```

When auditors test change management, they sample production changes and ask to see the approved record behind each one. A commit that can't be linked to a record is the finding, whatever the record says.

pattern.description: Regular expression a work item reference must match. The default matches Jira keys; use `#[0-9]+` for GitHub issues.

allowBranch.description: Whether a reference in the branch name covers every commit on it.

author-identity-domain.name: Commits come from a known identity
author-identity-domain.description: Every commit in the build range was authored and committed with an email address on a domain your organisation controls.
author-identity-domain.remediation:
Set your git identity to the email address your organisation issued, either for the repository or globally:

```bash
git config user.email dana@company.com
```

GitHub's `users.noreply.github.com` addresses are excluded by default because they can't be matched to an identity provider, and that match is what ties a commit to a person whose access can be recertified.

domains.description: Comma separated domains an address may be on. If empty, the guardrail skips, because it can't know your domains.

allowBots.description: Whether an address ending in `[bot]@users.noreply.github.com` is accepted, for commits authored by an app.

no-wip-commits.name: No work in progress commits
no-wip-commits.description: The build range contains no commit whose subject says it was never meant to be merged.
no-wip-commits.remediation:
Clean up the range before merging:

```bash
git rebase --interactive --autosquash origin/main
```

`--autosquash` folds `fixup!` and `squash!` commits into the commits they name. A `WIP` commit on a protected branch is a change nobody described, which is the same evidence problem as a commit with no work item.

markers.description: Comma separated markers that mark a commit subject as work in progress.

changed-lines-budget.name: The change is few enough lines to review
changed-lines-budget.description: The build range adds and removes few enough lines that a reviewer can read the whole change before approving it.
changed-lines-budget.remediation:
Split the change, or land it as a stack of pull requests that are each small enough to read. Review quality drops sharply as more lines are put in front of a reviewer, and an approval on a change nobody could read makes review a control that exists on paper only.

If the lines are unavoidable (a generated file, a lock file, a formatting pass or a mass rename), list those paths in `ignore` so only the lines a reviewer reads are counted. Otherwise, raise `maxLines` for that run instead of removing the guardrail, so the exception stays visible.

Binary files have no line count and are not counted.

maxLines.description: Maximum number of lines the range may add and remove combined.

ignore.description: Comma separated globs excluded from the count, for generated files and lock files a reviewer does not read line by line.

changed-files-budget.name: The change is small enough to review
changed-files-budget.description: The build range changes few enough files that a reviewer can hold the whole change in their head.
changed-files-budget.remediation:
Split the change. A review that can't be done properly is a control that exists on paper only, and reviewer attention drops sharply with size: an approval on a pull request touching a thousand files proves nothing.

If a large change is unavoidable (a rename, a generated file or a dependency bump), raise `maxFiles` for that run instead of removing the guardrail, so the exception stays visible.

maxFiles.description: Maximum number of files the range may change.

ignore.description: Comma separated globs excluded from the count, for generated files and lock files a reviewer does not read line by line.
